nameStory: This tiny weevil earned its "red-shouldered" name from the distinctive reddish-orange spots that adorn its dark body, looking like bright shoulder patches on a little beetle. The "leaf rolling" part comes from its remarkable parenting behavior — females carefully roll oak leaves into neat, cigar-shaped nurseries for their eggs, creating one of nature's most precise origami displays.
description: The Red-shouldered Leaf Rolling Weevil is a small, dark beetle about the size of a grain of rice, easily recognized by its characteristic long snout and bright reddish-orange spots. Like all weevils, it has a distinctive elongated "nose" called a rostrum that it uses for feeding and drilling holes for egg-laying. These industrious little beetles are most famous for their incredible leaf-rolling skills, transforming oak leaves into tightly wound green cylinders. You'll often spot their handiwork before you see the beetle itself — look for perfectly rolled leaves dangling from oak branches like tiny green scrolls.

idTips.label: Leaf Rolls
idTips.description: Look for tightly rolled oak leaves that feel firm and papery to the touch, hanging like small green cigars from branches — this is the weevil's signature calling card

idTips.label: Body Color and Spots
idTips.description: Dark brown to black body with two bright reddish-orange spots that stand out like tiny beacons — the spots have a slightly glossy sheen

idTips.label: Long Snout
idTips.description: Prominent curved rostrum (snout) that's nearly as long as the rest of its body, giving it a distinctive elephant-trunk appearance

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small beetle, typically about the size of a grain of rice or smaller — you may need to look closely to spot the red shoulder patches

idTips.label: Oak Association
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near oak trees, particularly favoring the younger, more tender leaves that are easier to roll and manipulate

habitat: You'll find these weevils in oak forests, woodlands, and anywhere oak trees grow throughout New England, from suburban yards with mature oaks to mixed hardwood forests. They prefer areas with healthy oak populations, especially where you can find red, white, or black oak species. Look for them in both lowland and upland oak habitats, from sea level to moderate elevations in our region's hills and mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and begin their leaf-rolling activity as oak leaves unfurl — this is prime time to spot both the beetles and their fresh, green leaf rolls.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you'll see the most leaf rolls and adult beetles. The rolled leaves from spring may start to brown and become more noticeable hanging from branches.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down, and many of the season's leaf rolls will have turned brown and may still be hanging from branches as evidence of their summer work.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in leaf litter and bark crevices, so you won't see active beetles, but old brown leaf rolls may persist on branches as winter reminders of their craftsmanship.

funFact: Female weevils are master engineers who can roll an entire oak leaf into a perfect cylinder in just 20-30 minutes, using their legs like tiny hands to fold and tuck the leaf while secreting a natural glue to hold it together — creating a weatherproof nursery that protects their single egg inside from both predators and the elements.
confusionNotes: The leaf rolls themselves are unmistakable, but the tiny beetles might be confused with other small weevils on oak trees. Remember the bright red shoulder spots — if you see perfectly rolled oak leaves but the beetle lacks those distinctive reddish-orange patches, you're looking at a different species. The rolled leaves are your best identification clue since they're much easier to spot than the beetles themselves.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these beneficial leaf-rollers with harmful pest weevils — while they do use oak leaves for reproduction, they rarely cause significant damage to healthy trees and are actually fascinating examples of insect engineering. The name can be confusing since they're sometimes called "oak leafrolling weevils" in field guides, but "red-shouldered" better describes their most distinctive visual feature.
compareHints: Since this is the only Synolabus species in our dataset for New England, compare it with other leaf-rolling weevils in the Attelabidae family. Other leaf-rolling weevils may create similar rolls but typically lack the distinctive bright red-orange shoulder spots that make this species unmistakable. The combination of oak preference, precise leaf-rolling behavior, and those bright shoulder patches sets this species apart from its relatives.
